summary: Describes the Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys protocol, which sets up and maintains security associations using Kerberos for authentication. It reuses IKE Quick Mode payloads, so IKE implementations can be mostly reused. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets two computers set up a secure connection by using a trusted ticket office, instead of doing heavy math themselves.

questions: how does kink use kerberos for ipsec
subtitle: How two hosts use Kerberos tickets to set up IPsec security associations in as few as two messages.

tldr.problem: IKE sets up IPsec keys with public key operations and peer-to-peer policy, which is costly and hard to manage in a centrally administered network.
tldr.mechanism: KINK authenticates peers with Kerberos tickets and carries IKE Quick Mode payloads inside its own small command and reply messages, so a security association can be created in two messages.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track protocol that trades the cost of IKE for dependence on a Kerberos KDC, and it inherits the weaknesses of both Kerberos and IKE.

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: CREATE, DELETE, REPLY, GETTGT, ACK, STATUS

today: RFC 4430 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself notes that IKEv2 does not use Quick Mode, so using IKEv2 with KINK would need extra work described there.

sections.title: Why KINK Exists
sections.content:
KINK (Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys) is meant for a centrally managed environment where security policy has to stay consistent. Its goals are privacy, authentication and replay protection of key management messages, and avoiding denial of service where possible. It also aims for low computational cost, low latency and a small footprint, and it avoids or minimizes public key operations.

The RFC contrasts this with IKE. IKE is peer-to-peer, so each peer must know a site's policy, and it relies on Diffie-Hellman and X.509 certificates, which are computationally expensive. IKE with pre-shared keys needs key distribution between all peers, which the RFC calls an O(n^2) problem. With Kerberos, keys live in the KDC, so the number of principal keys is O(n+m) for n clients and m servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Passing secret handshakes between every pair of friends takes forever. It is easier if one trusted office knows everyone and vouches for them.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
KINK is a command/response protocol that can create, delete and maintain IPsec security associations (SAs). Each message has a common header and a list of type-length-value payloads. KINK itself is stateless in the sense that a command or response needs no hard state stored for KINK. This differs from IKE, which first builds an ISAKMP SA in Main Mode and then runs Quick Mode exchanges.

Kerberos provides mutual authentication and replay protection. Before talking to a peer, a host needs a service ticket for it from the KDC. For SA creation, the payloads that follow the Kerberos AP-REQ payload are encrypted. KINK reuses the IKE Quick Mode payloads of section 5.5 of the IKE specification, so existing IKE code can be largely reused. Authenticated exchanges are required before any public key operation or state installation, which limits denial of service.

When a peer has no key shared with the KDC, which is typical with PKINIT, KINK can use the Kerberos User-to-User mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: KINK is a short conversation: one side asks, the other answers. The pass from the ticket office proves who is who, so nobody has to keep long notes.

sections.title: Message Flows
sections.content:
Every flow is a command, a response, and in CREATE flows an optional acknowledgement. A command is GETTGT, CREATE, DELETE or STATUS. The response is REPLY and the acknowledgement is ACK.

CREATE is optimistic. The initiator creates an inbound SA and puts its optimistic proposal in the first transform of the first proposal. If the responder picks it, two messages are enough (a 2-way handshake). If the responder chooses another proposal, adds a nonce or accepts a key exchange (KE) payload, it MUST set the ACKREQ bit and the exchange becomes a 3-way handshake. The responder may lower LIFE_KILOBYTES and LIFE_SECONDS but must not raise them.

In a two-message exchange the responder contributes no keying material. The RFC says the KDC is a reliable source of randomness, which often makes the session key adequate, and that this is a trade-off between key strength and message count left to policy.

DELETE is pessimistic: the initiator keeps its inbound SA until the reply arrives. KINK does not allow half-open SAs, so the responder MUST delete both directions. An implementation SHOULD use a grace timer of at least two times the average round-trip time.

STATUS sends or elicits information such as notifications and is also used for dead peer detection. GETTGT fetches a peer's ticket-granting ticket for User-to-User authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: To set up a secret line, one side makes an offer and starts using it right away, hoping the other agrees. If they disagree, there is one extra message to settle it.

sections.title: Message and Payload Format
sections.content:
All values use network byte order. The KINK header has Type, a 4-bit major version (MUST be 1), Length, a DOI (domain of interpretation; the IPsec DOI is 1), a transaction ID (XID), NextPayload, the A (ACKREQ) bit and CksumLen, followed by payloads and a checksum. The XID ties a command, reply and optional ACK together and lets the initiator tell outstanding requests apart. It is not used for replay protection, because Kerberos does that.

The Cksum is a Kerberos keyed checksum (get_mic) over the whole message, computed with the session key in the ticket. A CksumLen of zero means the message is unauthenticated. If verification fails, the message MUST be dropped. Headers, payloads and the checksum are aligned on 4-octet boundaries.

Payload types are KINK_AP_REQ, KINK_AP_REP, KINK_KRB_ERROR, KINK_TGT_REQ, KINK_TGT_REP, KINK_ISAKMP, KINK_ENCRYPT and KINK_ERROR. The AP-REQ and AP-REP payloads carry an EPOCH and a raw Kerberos message. KINK_ISAKMP wraps IKE Quick Mode payloads, with a new ISAKMP header for each discrete SA operation. KINK_ENCRYPT must be the last outer payload, and it is encrypted before the final checksum is applied.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a label on the front saying what it is and who it is for, then the contents, then a seal at the end that shows nobody tampered with it.

sections.title: Differences from IKE Quick Mode
sections.content:
KINK uses ISAKMP payloads directly, specifically IKE phase 2 (Quick Mode) payloads. Unless the RFC says otherwise, all IKE capabilities and requirements MUST be supported, and IKE phase 1 payloads MUST NOT be sent.

  • The SA payload uses DOI 1 and situation SIT_IDENTITY_ONLY.
  • The HASH payload is not used.
  • The responder nonce Nr is optional, which enables optimistic keying.
  • Identification payloads are limited to IPv4 and IPv6 address, subnet and range types.
  • Perfect forward secrecy through the KE payload is relaxed from must implement to SHOULD implement.

Key material is derived as in IKE, using KEYMAT = prf(SKEYID_d, [g(qm)^xy |] protocol | SPI | Ni_b [| Nr_b]). Here the prf follows the Kerberos session key's etype and SKEYID_d is the session key from the service ticket. A missing Nr is treated as a zero-length value.
sections.plainLanguage: KINK borrows the second half of the old handshake and throws away the heavy first half, because the ticket already proved who everyone is.

sections.title: Rekeying, Dead Peers and Transport
sections.content:
The initiator of an SA is responsible for rekeying it. There are no special rekey semantics: the initiator CREATEs a new SA and then deletes the old one or lets it time out. The soft lifetime MUST be randomized to avoid synchronization.

For dead peer detection, each peer records an epoch for the other and reflects its own epoch in every AP-REQ and AP-REP. A changed epoch means the peer lost its SA database, so all SAs from it are invalid. A STATUS message elicits a protected, replay-protected reply that shows whether the peer is alive and whether its epoch changed. This is not periodic keepalive, and a peer MUST NOT conclude a peer is dead only from unprotected ICMP messages.

KINK runs over UDP on port 910. It has one retransmission timer T with truncated exponential back-off. Because Kerberos needs fresh authenticators, each retransmission is rebuilt with a new authenticator and checksum, but it MUST reuse the same ticket. Clock skew beyond the policy limit (usually 5 minutes) gets KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers sometimes check that the other side is still there and has not forgotten the secret line. If it forgot, they set it up again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
KINK names Kerberos principals, but the traffic it protects is identified by selectors such as IP addresses. If two hosts claim the same IP address, it may be impossible to say which principal's key protects the data, so implementations must take care with that binding.

KINK inherits the weaknesses of Kerberos and IKE. The KDC is a point of attack, and it must supply adequate entropy for session keys. Kerberos user passwords may face dictionary attacks, so the RFC recommends randomly generated keys for service principals. Kerberos does not generally give perfect forward secrecy. KINK can provide it with the KE payload, but that is optional because of its cost.

Errors sent without cryptographic protection must be handled carefully, to balance being helpful against being used in a denial of service attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket office is a single place everyone trusts, so it must be guarded well. Also, someone must double-check who really owns each address.
